# Preface

Hello and welcome to the SimSN community\! We’re thrilled to have you as one of our users. This document will walk you through all the basics of running your new basketball team, from requesting an available team to recruiting to setting player minutes and gameplan. We also have a very active Discord which is a great place to hang out with other users and ask any questions you have.

Our site runs sims for both college and pro basketball. College teams are run by a single user and there are many teams available; pro teams are run by one or more users filling the roles of owner, general manager (GM), coach, and scout. Almost all NBA teams currently have active owners, but you are welcome to reach out to them to request a position on their staff.

This document starts with general football information that applies to both levels, then splits into separate sections for player acquisition (recruiting for college, drafting/trading/free agency for pro).

_Note: This document is a work in progress but does cover the basics for SimCBB. SimNBA section is still in progress._

# Steps for Signing Up

You can find a list of all current owners and their teams on the Available Teams page. Any team or role with a blue “Request” button is in need of a user. Once you’ve submitted a request, a post is created in the job-applications subforum and an admin will be around to approve your request. For college, your conference commissioner will be along shortly to approve your application. For Pro, you may want to reach out to the owner directly and ask if they are accepting staff applications.

# Basketball Engine

_A coach-facing overview of the possession-by-possession simulation engine and how players, lineups, strategies, and game situations interact.._

The new SimBBAv4 engine transforms the game of SimSN basketball from a relay of shots, to a flowing series of events across the basketball court, from dribbles to passing to fouls to shots and rebounds. Besides the expanded simulation, new features have been added to increase the depth and realism of the game.

# 1. How a Game Is Simulated

A game begins with the opening tip and continues action by action. Every action consumes game-clock and shot-clock time. The offense may move, pass, shoot, or lose possession. The defense may cut off movement, pressure a pass, force a turnover, block a shot, commit a foul, or secure a rebound.

The ball occupies a real location on the simulated court. Court position determines which shots are available, which defensive attribute is most relevant, how difficult a pass may be, and how close the offense is to the basket.

Possessions do not have a fixed number of actions. A team may shoot early, pass several times, drive toward the basket, reset after being cut off, or run the shot clock deep. This is where pace, player preferences, BBIQ, and formations become visible.

## College and professional games

College games use halves, college foul and bonus rules, college media-timeout windows, and the college shot clock. Professional games use quarters, professional foul-out limits, professional timeout allocations, and the professional shot clock. Overtime is handled automatically whenever regulation ends tied.

# 2. Player Attributes

Player attributes describe what a player is capable of doing when the engine asks them to perform a specific action. A strong attribute improves the relevant contest, but the result also depends on the defender, fatigue, momentum, location, and game situation.

## Scoring attributes

**Finishing**

Finishing governs shots close to the basket, including inside and paint attempts. Strong finishers are better equipped to convert drives, post opportunities, and other close-range chances.

**2pt Shooting**

2pt Shooting governs midrange attempts. It matters when an offense creates space between the paint and three-point line.

**3pt Shooting**

3pt Shooting governs attempts from behind the arc, including corner threes. It also helps determine which player is trusted with a desperate last-second heave.

**Free Throw**

Free Throw governs foul-shot accuracy. Fatigue can reduce a player’s effectiveness at the line late in games.

## Ball movement attributes

**Ballwork**

Ballwork represents the ability to handle and pass the ball under pressure. Strong Ballwork helps a player complete difficult passes and helps the lineup protect the ball against the opposing defense.

**Agility**

Agility governs a player’s ability to advance or reposition the ball when challenged by a defender. It is central to drives, cuts, transition movement, and escaping pressure.

## Defensive attributes

**Interior Defense**

Interior Defense is used against movement and shots near the basket. It is especially important against teams that attack the paint or rely on strong finishers.

**Perimeter Defense**

Perimeter Defense is used against actions farther from the basket, including three-point areas and much of transition play.

**Interior and Perimeter Defense together**

Midrange defense blends both defensive attributes. A versatile defender who is competent in both areas is better equipped to handle players moving between zones.

**Block**

Block affects the chance of rejecting a shot. Shot location and the height difference between shooter and defender also matter.

**Rebounding**

Rebounding contributes to the five-player lineup’s ability to win missed shots. Strong rebounding lineups create extra possessions and limit the opponent’s second chances.

**Stealing**

Stealing represents takeaway ability on the player profile. In the current engine, turnovers and steals are influenced primarily through the broader lineup and possession system rather than being a simple one-rating check.

## Mental and physical attributes

**Basketball IQ (BBIQ)**

BBIQ represents awareness and decision-making. It helps players recognize the shot clock, avoid offensive fouls, defend without fouling, and respond correctly in late-clock or late-game situations.

**Height**

Height influences tipoffs and shot-blocking matchups.

**Stamina**

Stamina represents the amount of effective playing time a player can handle. A player with high Stamina can remain useful deeper into heavy minutes; a low-Stamina player may become exhausted even with fewer total minutes.

# 3. Lineups and Strings

Each team builds three strings from five positional lineup rows: two Guards, two Forwards, and one Center. The first string supplies the starters, while the second and third strings supply the primary rotation.

The Usage value attached to a lineup assignment helps determine how likely that player is to be selected when substitutions occur. Usage does not guarantee exact minutes and does not directly tell the player how often to shoot.

Important to note: The First String is ALWAYS the starting lineup, regardless of their usage weight.

## Substitution logic

At an ordinary substitution opportunity, the engine chooses eligible players by position using the lineup’s Usage settings. A player cannot occupy two places in the same on-court lineup, even if that player appears in multiple lineup assignments.

If foul-outs or foul-protection restrictions exhaust a position group, the engine can use an eligible player from another position. This fallback prevents the simulation from failing when a team must play an unconventional lineup.

## Why lineup combinations matter

The engine evaluates the five players who are actually on the floor. Substitutions can change ball security, rebounding, defensive strength, fatigue, and the team’s preferred shot locations immediately. A bench unit may therefore play with a noticeably different identity than the starters.

# 4. Player Shot Preferences

Every lineup assignment includes Inside, Mid, and Three proportions. These values describe a player’s preferred offensive role and must total 100\.

The proportions serve two connected purposes. First, the five active players combine to create the lineup’s team-level shot identity. Second, each individual player’s preferences determine how willing that player is to shoot after receiving the ball in a particular zone.

## How the lineup guides the ball

If the active five collectively favor inside scoring, movement and passing are more likely to develop toward the paint and basket. If the lineup favors three-point shooting, the offense is more likely to develop toward perimeter locations. The chosen offensive and defensive formations modify these tendencies.

## How the player decides to shoot

Once the ball reaches a shooting area, the ballhandler’s preference is compared with the preferences of the active lineup. A player who is especially willing to shoot from that area is more likely to take the opportunity. A reluctant player is more likely to move or pass.

Preferences affect shot selection, not shot accuracy. A player can be eager to attempt a shot without being good at making it.

## How preferences affect receiving passes

Clean passes mildly favor teammates whose preferences fit the destination. An interior-oriented player is more likely to receive a pass developing toward the basket, while a perimeter-oriented player is more likely to receive a pass developing outside.

_The old team-level Inside, Mid, and Three gameplan proportions are no longer part of the engine’s decision-making. Team identity now emerges from the players currently on the court._

# 5. Pace

Pace controls how quickly a team tries to operate and how much physical strain that style places on its players. The available choices are Very Slow, Slow, Balanced, Fast, and Very Fast.

**Very Slow**

Uses the longest action profile, preserves the most Stamina, and generally waits deepest into the shot clock before urgency develops.

**Slow**

Leans toward deliberate actions and provides a moderate Stamina benefit.

**Balanced**

Uses neutral action timing, Stamina, and shot-clock behavior.

**Fast**

Leans toward quicker actions and earlier shot-clock urgency, with a moderate reduction in available Stamina.

**Very Fast**

Most strongly favors quick actions and early shot-clock urgency, but creates the greatest Stamina cost.

## Pace does not dictate every possession

A Very Fast team will not always perform the fastest possible action, and a Very Slow team will not always use the slowest. Pace changes the likelihood of different action speeds, allowing natural possession-to-possession variation.

## Coaching tradeoff

Faster teams can create more possessions and pressure a slower opponent, but they may tire sooner and take more early-clock shots. Slower teams can conserve energy and develop possessions, but they may face greater late-clock pressure if the offense stalls.

# 6. Offensive Formations

Offensive formation influences where movement and passing try to develop. Formation combines with the active players’ preferences; it does not replace them.

**Balanced**

Applies no special positional emphasis. This is the best choice for a neutral approach or a team still discovering its identity.

**Motion**

Encourages fluid movement with a modest preference for inside and three-point development. It gives up some offensive-rebounding presence.

**Pick-and-Roll**

Encourages inside and midrange development while reducing the emphasis on three-point destinations. It also sacrifices some offensive-rebounding presence.

**Post-Up**

Most strongly encourages inside development and improves offensive-rebounding presence. It gives up some midrange and perimeter emphasis.

**Space-and-Post**

Encourages midrange and three-point development while reducing inside emphasis. It also sacrifices some offensive-rebounding presence.

## Formation and personnel

A formation is most effective when it complements the players on the floor. Post-Up cannot turn poor finishers into elite interior scorers, and Space-and-Post cannot make weak shooters accurate. The formation helps the offense seek particular areas; player ratings determine whether those chances succeed.

# 7. Defensive Formations

Defensive formation changes which offensive destinations are encouraged or discouraged and can influence the opponent’s offensive-rebounding environment. Every defense gives something up.

**Man-to-Man**

Uses neutral zone tendencies and allows a selected Focus Player to be double-teamed.

**1-3-1 Zone**

Discourages midrange development but can open more inside and perimeter opportunities. It may also concede additional offensive-rebounding chances.

**3-2 Zone**

Discourages three-point development but can open more inside and midrange opportunities. It may concede additional offensive-rebounding chances.

**2-3 Zone**

Discourages inside development and improves the defense’s rebounding position, but can open more midrange and three-point opportunities.

**Box-and-One Zone**

Uses a neutral general zone profile while applying the strongest special attention to a selected Focus Player. The commitment can create opportunities for the other four offensive players.

## Focus Player

Man-to-Man and Box-and-One can designate an opposing player for special attention. When that player is on the court, the double team makes that player’s shots, movement, and passing more difficult.

Committing a second defender creates smaller advantages for the other offensive players. They receive more room to move, pass, and shoot. Box-and-One applies a stronger version of both the pressure and the teammate tradeoff.

If the selected Focus Player is not participating, belongs to a different opponent, or is currently on the bench, the engine safely ignores the focus setting until the correct player is on the floor.

# 8. Movement and On-Ball Defense

Movement represents a ballhandler trying to reach another legal area of the court. The desired location is selected from the court state, direction of play, lineup preferences, and formation matchup.

The ballhandler’s Agility is contested by the defender’s appropriate defensive ability. Perimeter Defense is most important outside, Interior Defense is most important near the basket, and both contribute in the midrange.

An offense can still succeed against a better defender, and a defender can still stop a superior athlete. Large rating differences matter, but movement is never automatic.

Before the movement contest, the engine can identify an offensive foul or a non-shooting defensive foul. A successful move changes the court position; a failed move leaves the ballhandler in place.

# 9. Passing

Passing is both a location decision and a player contest. The offense first chooses a legal target area. Shorter and more natural passes are favored, while long cross-court passes carry more risk.

Ballwork helps the passer execute the play. The defender’s appropriate defense applies pressure based on where the pass is developing. A clean pass reaches the target and selects a receiver whose preferences fit that location.

## Deflections and loose balls

A pressured or ambitious pass can be deflected. The offense may recover the loose ball and continue, or the defense may recover it for a turnover and steal. Long-distance passes are naturally more vulnerable.

## Passing and assists

The player making the most recent clean pass becomes the potential assister. One movement action may occur before the shot without removing the assist. A second movement, another pass, a turnover, or another possession-changing interruption removes or replaces that assist opportunity.

# 10. Shooting

A player can shoot only after the ball reaches a legal frontcourt shooting area. The shot type is determined by location: inside, paint, midrange, three, or corner three.

Shot success begins with the player’s relevant scoring attribute. The defender then applies a limited adjustment using the defense appropriate for that zone. Fatigue, positive momentum, shot-clock quality, home court, and an active double team can also contribute.

## Defensive impact

A weak defender can improve the shooter’s chance and a strong defender can reduce it, but defense is deliberately prevented from making an ordinary attempt impossible. The shooter’s own ability remains the foundation of accuracy.

## Early and late shots

Extremely early shots receive a quality penalty because the offense has not allowed the possession to develop. Desperation shots late in the clock also receive a penalty. Pace and BBIQ affect how quickly the offense becomes willing to shoot as the clock approaches zero.

## Blocks

Blocks resolve separately from ordinary shot accuracy. Close shots are more blockable than perimeter attempts. The defender’s Block rating, fatigue, shot location, and height relative to the shooter all contribute.

## Dunks

Especially strong successful inside attempts can become dunks. Strong paint attacks can become drive dunks, while the most dominant paint results can become poster dunks over the defender. Dunks count as normal two-point makes but generate stronger momentum.

## Last-second heaves

With only a few seconds remaining, a tied team or a team trailing by three or fewer can attempt a final cross-court heave. This can occur after an inbound, steal, defensive rebound, or pass, but not directly from a tipoff. The attempt consumes the remaining clock.

# 11. Fouls and Free Throws

The engine distinguishes shooting fouls, non-shooting defensive fouls, and offensive fouls. Foul risk depends on court location and BBIQ.

## Shooting fouls

Contact is more common near the basket than on perimeter shots. A defender with strong BBIQ is less likely to commit a shooting foul. Made shots can produce an and-one; missed attempts produce the appropriate number of free throws.

## Non-shooting fouls

Non-shooting fouls are tracked as team fouls. In college, the bonus and double bonus are awarded according to the defending team’s foul count for the half.

## Offensive fouls

A ballhandler can be called for a charge while attempting to move. High offensive BBIQ reduces this risk, while a high-BBIQ defender is better at drawing the foul. An offensive foul is a turnover.

## Free throws

Free throws use the player’s Free Throw rating, current fatigue, and home-court context. Momentum does not improve free-throw ability.

## Foul-outs

College players are disqualified after five personal fouls and professional players after six. The engine removes a disqualified player immediately and finds a legal substitute, using the fallback pool if necessary.

# 12. Foul Protection

Foul Protection is an automatic coaching instruction designed to keep important players from reaching disqualification too early.

**Off**

No player is automatically removed because of first-half or second-half foul accumulation.

**Protected Player**

The selected player is benched after reaching two fouls in a half and cannot return until the next half.

**Fouls per Half**

Every player is protected at the selected foul threshold. A player reaching that number is benched until the next half.

Foul Protection is removed during the final two minutes of the final regulation period and throughout overtime. At that point, the engine allows the coach’s best available players to return despite their foul risk.

# 13. Rebounding

Rebounding is first resolved as a five-player lineup contest. Strong rebounding units are more likely to earn second chances and finish defensive possessions.

Offensive and defensive formations can improve or weaken rebounding position. Post-Up helps the offense attack the glass, while a 2-3 Zone helps the defense protect it.

An offensive rebound keeps possession and applies the shorter offensive-rebound shot-clock reset. A defensive rebound changes possession and restores the full shot clock.

# 14. Stamina and Exhaustion

Stamina measures how much effective playing time a player can handle. Exhaustion is based on playing time relative to that player’s available Stamina, not simply on raw minutes.

A player with many minutes and excellent Stamina may remain effective, while a player with fewer minutes and poor Stamina may already be exhausted. Fatigue grows progressively and becomes more severe after a player exceeds their available capacity.

## What fatigue affects

Fatigue reduces player-specific technical and physical checks, including shooting, finishing, free throws, ballwork, agility, defense, and blocking.

## What fatigue does not affect

Fatigue does not reduce BBIQ, Height, coaching strategy, formations, or fixed game events.

## Breathers

Halftime, quarter breaks, overtime breaks, media timeouts, and team timeouts restore partial effective energy. Recovery reduces the fatigue burden but does not erase actual minutes from the box score.

# 15. Momentum

Momentum behaves like a pendulum between the two teams. Made shots, dunks, steals, and blocks move momentum toward the successful team. Missed shots move it away from the team that missed.

Only the team holding momentum receives a benefit. The other team is not penalized. Momentum can improve shooting, movement, and passing, but it is intentionally limited so that a hot team does not automatically win every check.

Dunks and three-point makes create larger swings than ordinary two-point makes, and poster dunks create the strongest scoring swing.

## Stopping a run

Halftime, quarter breaks, overtime breaks, media timeouts, and team timeouts pull momentum back toward neutral by different amounts. This gives automatic timeout strategy an important role in managing opponent runs.

# 16. Media Timeouts

## College

College media timeouts occur at the first eligible stoppage after the clock passes 16:00, 12:00, 8:00, and 4:00 in each regulation half. College overtime has no media timeouts.

## Professional

Professional media timeout windows occur during each regulation quarter around the under-seven and under-three marks, depending on timeout activity in that quarter.

## What a media timeout does

A media timeout provides partial fatigue recovery, slows momentum, and creates an ordinary substitution opportunity. It does not force the starters back into the game.

## Timeout conversion

If an automatic team timeout would occur shortly before an untaken media timeout, the stoppage becomes the media timeout instead. The team keeps its timeout.

# 17. Team Timeouts

College teams receive four regulation timeouts and one additional timeout per overtime. Professional teams receive seven regulation timeouts and two additional timeouts per overtime.

During live play, only the team with possession can call a timeout. The defensive team may call one only during an eligible dead-ball stoppage, such as after a foul or when the ball is out of bounds.

## Opponent Lead Timeout

When enabled, the team requests a timeout after the opponent’s lead reaches the configured threshold. This can interrupt a run, create substitutions, and provide partial recovery.

## Designated Player Exhaustion

When enabled, the engine monitors the selected player while that player is on the floor. The team requests a timeout after the player reaches the chosen exhaustion level.

## Team Exhaustion

When enabled, the engine averages exhaustion across the five current players. The team requests a timeout when the on-court average reaches the selected level.

## Preserve Timeouts

When enabled, the team saves its final timeout until the last two minutes of regulation. Automatic triggers cannot spend that timeout earlier. The restriction is removed in the final two minutes and in overtime.

## Back-to-back protection

Automatic triggers cannot repeatedly call timeouts without the triggering condition first clearing, and a live action must occur before another automatic timeout can be taken.

# 18. Substitutions During Free Throws

The engine protects the active free-throw sequence while still allowing realistic substitution opportunities.

Media-timeout substitutions and defensive foul-out substitutions occur before the free throws begin. An and-one permits substitutions before the single attempt. On a multi-shot foul, substitutions can occur between the first and second attempts but are not repeated before a third.

If the front end of a one-and-one is missed, the ball becomes live immediately and no substitution is triggered.

# 19. Shot Clock and Late-Game Behavior

Shot probability gradually increases as the clock approaches zero, but the engine never forces a shot. A team can still pass, move, or make a mistake at the end of the clock.

Pace determines when the offense begins feeling urgency, while BBIQ influences how well the ballhandler recognizes the situation. Faster teams become willing to shoot earlier; slower teams try to work deeper into the possession.

Extremely early and desperation shots can suffer quality penalties even when the offense is willing to take them.

## Overtime

A tie at the end of regulation automatically triggers overtime. Teams receive additional timeouts, partial fatigue recovery, and a new tipoff. Overtime continues until a period ends with a winner.

# Management Tools

Once you’re set up on the interface, you can view your Roster to see the names, positions, experience level (school year / years pro) and Overall grade for all your players. You can click on any column to sort by that column, or click on a player name to get a pop-up with their letter grade for all applicable skills. There’s also an Export button to download everything in a .csv file.

Note that college players have letter grades which cover a range of values, while pro players have their exact numbers revealed. This simulates that college players’ true abilities are less well-known than their professional counterparts. Letter grades are relative across all players \- meaning that a PG’s A grade for 3pt shooting will be a very similar value to a SF’s A grade in 3pt shooting.

The numerical range possible across both basketball leagues is between 1-50. For college basketball, the most typical range for a player’s attributes will be between 1-30.

## Gameplan

On the gameplan page, teams are able to adjust their starting, 2nd string, and 3rd string lineups by position. Each position is designated three lineup spots, and designates a specific spot on the court.

The default lineup is the following: C, F, F, G, G

A center, two forwards, and two guards.

From these positions, teams are able to add any players to the following spots:

- Center: Centers & Forwards
- Forward: Centers, Forwards, and Guards
- Guard: Forwards and Guards

This gives teams the flexibility of setting up their offense how they choose to, allowing teams to run a Jumbo-style lineup, small ball, or even micro-ball lineup.

**Pace** is the speed of which a possession will play out when your team has possession of the ball. It also determines how many actions take place before a player decides to shoot. Selecting fast pace may get the offense to make decisions quicker and attempt shots faster, but it does wear down stamina over-time. Additionally, a slower paced offense will take their time, reducing the amount of stamina lost in a possession, but it will also cause time to run down faster.

**Usage** tracks how much time the player will spend on the court within their current position. Usage is rated between 1 and 10, 1 being the lowest and 10 being the highest. Players with higher usage will see the court more often.

**Shot Allocation** is split between **Inside, Mid,** and **Three Point Proportion**. Allocation determines that if the player is in a specific part of the court where that type of shot can be made, they will decide to make it. Additionally, if the player isn’t in a part of the court for the shot that they **_want_** to make, they may move to that part of the court to set up a shot. Shot Allocation is related to the player only, and all three ranges must equate to 100 per player. Additionally, no shot allocation may be more than 50%.

Once changes have been made to your lineup and gameplan, it is best to save your changes. Remember: Gameplans must be completed by **11:59 PM on the night before games are played** to be used in the upcoming week’s games. So, make sure to save your gameplans by Sunday Nights for Monday games; Tuesday Nights for Wednesday games; Thursday Nights for Friday games; and Friday Nights for Saturday games.

You can (and should) make minor changes to your gameplan as the season goes along.

Now that we’ve covered the basics, let’s discuss how you acquire and develop new players. These are different depending on which league you’re joining. We’ll start with college recruiting and then dive into the (more complex) pro sim after that.

## Roster Page

The roster page shows the full roster of your team, your player health, attributes, and team information. Additionally, you may also view the rosters of other teams that exist within your league.

Users are able to conduct actions related to their players. For SimCBB, users may designate redshirts, cut players, or commit promises directly from the roster page. For SimNBA, teams may be able to cut players, move players to the G-League, trade players, and even offer extensions.

In addition, users are also able to export their roster and other rosters into a CSV file.

## Stats Page

Users may be able to view current season and previous season stats related to the respective league in which they manage their teams. Full player and team stats are readily viewable, along with individual game stats by week and game day. Additionally, users are able to export these stats as a csv.

## Building your roster

This documentation does go into detail further on roster building, but we will also highlight it here: for SimCBB, users will use the Recruiting page & Transfer Portal page to build their roster. Each page serves a separate roster-building method: one for the middle of the season, and one for the offseason. Recruiting high school talent will get you younger players with a higher ceiling, while the transfer portal allows you to acquire college-level talent in the middle of their collegiate career; albeit, it is also more risky.

For SimNBA, teams will use the Free Agency page to sign veteran players to their team, and the SimNBA draft page to draft & sign rookie talent to their team. Additionally, SimNBA teams may use the trade functionality on the NBA Team page to exchange players & draft picks for other players & draft picks.

## Player Cards

On most pages, users can click on a player’s name and it will pop open a player card. Player cards share detailed information on the selected player from their name & historic info, player preferences & biases, and their attributes. Additionally, career stats can be viewed for the player directly from the player card.

**Interlude: Feedback**

But before we split on league specific rules, here are links to the various feedback forums where you can share ideas or report issues. Please do not message admins directly or tag them on Discord for one-off questions; use the feedback forums or the \#mentor-help channel.

# College Basketball Exclusive Rules

### Player Acquisition - Recruiting

Every year the sim generates thousands of high school seniors, and users compete to get these new stars to sign with their program. The Recruiting Overview on the interface shows the names and positions of all these “croots”, along with a Star rating from 1-5, an Overall grade, a Potential grade, and their residing location (city, state, country). You can use the filters at the top to focus on certain positions, certain star levels, etc. If you see a player you’re interested in, click the green plus sign and he will be added to your recruiting board. No one can see your board except you.

A note on grades: “Overall” is the recruit’s current ability, while “Potential” represents the chance that a recruit will improve _from their current state_ over time. A player with A Potential will get better faster, but that doesn’t mean they are destined to become an “A” Overall player. Similarly, a B overall player with C- Potential isn’t “overperforming”, but simply will improve slower than average.

Recruiting takes place over 15 weeks of the regular season (real time). Every week a team gets 50 points to assign to recruits they are interested in; you can place anywhere from 1-20 points on a single player, and you can place points on as many players as you want. You must use whole numbers. You also have a number of scholarships you can offer; a player **must** get a scholarship offer from you to sign with your team. Scholarship offers are public knowledge (in the News section of the Interface, it will say a player has “received an offer” from that school), but points are hidden. _You can revoke a scholarship at any time, but you will not have the option to re-offer one to the same recruit; he will never sign with you once you’ve revoked his scholarship._

Recruiting is due **Wednesday morning at 11:59 AM (EST).** Once that window closes, the points from all teams are applied to players. Points are recorded each week and accumulate over time. Starting in week 4, if a player’s cumulative points from all teams passes a certain threshold, they will commit to one school based on a % chance. The threshold changes weekly depending on the number of interested teams (more teams, higher threshold, so the recruit will take longer to decide) and the week (later week, lower threshold, recruits will start signing for fewer points). Recruits also have a “tendency” that can affect this (Signs Early, Signs Late, etc). On week 20, all remaining recruits with any points will sign.

A team’s chances on a deciding player depend on how many points they’ve spent compared to other teams. While you can’t see the exact numbers, you can click on the Info button for any recruit to get a general idea of each team’s chances. If one team has a majority of the total points on a recruit they are a Strong Favorite; a team within 66% of the leader’s points is considered In Contention; a team under that threshold is Unlikely. Mathematically a recruit can only have one Strong Favorite (if they have one at all) but could have multiple teams In Contention. Once a recruit has decided, their final percentages are revealed.

“Scholarships Available” tells you how many players you can sign in this recruiting cycle. It is determined by how many players are leaving the program (via graduation or the transfer portal) compared to the roster limit of 100 players. The maximum class size is generally 7, but may be smaller or larger depending on the state of your roster.

You can offer more scholarships than you have spots available. If you run out of scholarship offers, you can’t send more until you either revoke some or until an offered player signs with a different school; when that happens you “get that offer back”, essentially. If you reach your class size limit in the middle of a recruiting sync, any further offers will be ignored.

## The Profile System

Based on the reception of the Profile System from our SimHockey simulation, we are introducing the Profile System to the SimCBB simulation.

The **Profile System** is a system that reflects the current state of a college athletic program in recruiting based on intangible and tangible attributes, while providing a numeric value in what a recruit may prefer for their college career. It is a prestige system designed to reward successful programs while giving other programs the chance to build based on both static attributes and the success of the conference.

Each college basketball team will have a set of nine attributes that are associated with the program's tangible and intangible attributes based on the quality of the school and the school’s facilities. Each attribute is rated between 1 and 10; 1 being the worst, 10 being the best rating.

Some attributes are dynamic; meaning that they will change every offseason based on team performance and graduating players. The remaining attributes are static due to them being qualities of the school that is being represented within the SimCBB league. These values will only change depending on if the school makes a change or an impact that correlates to one of the below attributes.

Each school will offer a different experience when recruiting with some schools being much easier to sign players with than others. For example, Kentucky, Indiana, Purdue, and Duke are powerhouse schools that will likely be the easiest to recruit for; whereas schools such as Stonehill, Lindenwood, St. Peter’s, and Canisius may have a more difficult time building their roster.

### Program Development

**Program Development** correlates to the team’s performance across the entire legacy of the sim. Meaning, depending on how the team teams from season to season, the team’s Program Development will dynamically change in each offseason.

With the introduction of the new system, each team’s Program Development attribute will be set to 5\.

### Professional Development

**Professional Development** correlates to how often players on the team are drafted into the SimNBA. The more players are drafted into the league, the higher the bonus acquired from Professional Development.

At the start of the inaugural season, each team’s Professional Development attribute will be set to 5\.

### Traditions

**Traditions** is a reflection of the team’s IRL counterpart within the actual NCAA D1 College Basketball sport. The more successful well-known teams are given a higher rating based on the following quantifiers:

- Win/Loss Record
- Conference Championships
- Playoff appearances
- NIT Championships
- National Championships

Tradition will be treated as a static value.

### Facilities

The **Facilities** attribute reflects the age of the IRL basketball program of the school but also on how up to date a program’s arena, practice facilities, and locker room are. Newer facilities in the IRL program will give the SimCBB team a higher rating.

Facilities will be treated as a static value.

### Atmosphere

**Atmosphere** ties into the gameday experience for both players and attendees at the school’s home arena. The rating between 1-10 ties into the program’s home arena capacity (1 point per 2000 attendees, with a minimum of 1 and maximum of 10\. The value will be rounded up based on the capacity of the arena.

Atmosphere will be treated as a static value.

### Academic Prestige

**Academic Prestige** is rating based on how well the school does academically IRL as both a school and the athletic program.

Given that a number of schools participating in SimCBB are very acclaimed universities, the Academic Prestige rating had to be balanced with a near-even amount of teams making up each possible rating when applicable.

### Coach Rating

Coach rating is a Dynamic attribute that correlates to the coach’s overall success in the sim. This variable will fluctuate at a slightly faster rate than program momentum and will equate to the coach’s success throughout their career within the sim.

New coaches entering the league will always have a CoachRating of 5\. Once the season ends, their W/L record through the season will be applied and will generate a new rating.

### Conference Prestige

Conference Rating is a dynamic attribute that correlates to the level of play that’s involved in the team’s conference. Recruits will have some bias regarding the conference they would like to play in, depending on how competitive the conference is.

For the inaugural implementation, each team’s Conference Rating is 5\. At the end of every season, each team’s conference rating will be adjusted based on the post-season performance of the conference members.

### Season Momentum

Season Momentum is a dynamic attribute that correlates to how well the team performed the previous season. Like Coach Rating, Season Momentum follows a similar practice but will instead only intake the W/L record of the previous season. In addition, if a team wins any big games such as a rivalry game or a playoff game, the score will adjust.

### Dynamic Adjustments to Attributes

Program Development and Professional Development at the moment are the only variables that will be dynamic from season to season.

Program Development reflects the team’s on-ice success, and professional development reflects the team’s success in their players being drafted into the professional league.

If a team goes winless in the regular season, their **program development** will decrease by 2 points.

If a team wins less than 25% of their total games in the regular season, their **program development** will decrease by 2 points.

If a team wins less than 50% of their total games in the regular season, their **program development** will decrease by 1 point.

If a team wins 75% of their regular season games, their **program development** increases by 1 point.

If a team goes undefeated in the regular season, their **program development** increases by 2 points.

If a team makes it to at least the Sweet 16 of the postseason tournament, their **program development** increases by 1 (non-stacking).

If a team makes it to the Final Four or is the runner-up, their **program development** increases by 2 (non-stacking).

The team that wins the national championship will have their **program development** increase by 3 (non-stacking).

A team that does not have any players drafted for more than one season will have their **professional development** decrease by 1\.

A team that has at least a player drafted in consecutive seasons will have their **professional development** increase by 1\.

A team that has at least 3 players drafted in consecutive seasons will have their **professional development** increase by 2\.

If all participating teams within a conference are defeated in the first round of the postseason tournament, their **conference prestige** will decrease by 1\.

If a team makes it to the Final Four or wins the national championship, their **conference prestige** will increase by 1\.

## Player Preferences

In the same way that each team has varying attributes, players will have their preference attributes that correlate to a team’s specific attribute. Preference attributes can range between 1 and 9; 1 being the lowest, 9 being the highest.

The player preference feature is in place instead of affinities to showcase the player’s preference regarding which kind of school they would like to play for.

Player preferences generated on each recruit will be on a normalized scale, with 5 being the expected average, with a standard deviation of 2\.

## Recruiting Points Formula

SimCBB uses team profile attributes and player preferences as part of a formula determining how impactful a team’s recruiting points are on a recruit.

The following formula compares each Team Attribute with the corresponding Player Preference attribute and forms an average using each attribute applicable. At the end of the formula, if the player is either close to home or is part of a pipeline, a small bonus is added onto the end of the modifier.

The first stage of the formula sets up a base modifier using the team attribute as a weight:  
![][image2]

The second stage of the formula calculates the adjusted modifier based on the difference between the team’s attribute, and the player’s preference. The greater the difference between the team attribute and the player preference, the more impactful the modifier. The higher the player preference, the less impactful the modifier becomes.

![][image3]

And the final multiplier is calculated by the following:  
![][image4]

If the recruit is close to home to the school, a 25% (0.25pt) bonus is applied onto the modifier. If the recruit is part of a pipeline and not close to home, a 15% (0.15pt) bonus is applied.

I’m going to showcase two examples on how the modifiers will work given a point submission of 10 points.

### Example 1

Duke is recruiting Test Testaverde, a Center located in North Dakota right outside Durham, NC. Below are Duke’s team attributes and Test Testaverde’s player attributes

|                 | Program | Prof. Dev. | Traditions | Facilities | Atmosphere | Academics | Conference | Coach | Season | CTH? | Avg    | Total  |
| :-------------- | ------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- | --------- | ---------- | ----- | ------ | ---- | ------ | ------ |
| Duke            | 5       | 5          | 10         | 9          | 10         | 7         | 5          | 5     | 5      | 0.25 |        |        |
| Test Testaverde | 5       | 5          | 5          | 5          | 5          | 5         | 5          | 5     | 5      |      |        |        |
|                 | 1       | 1          | 2          | 1.8        | 2          | 1.4       | 1          | 1     | 1      |      |        |        |
|                 | 1       | 1          | 1.5        | 1.4        | 1.5        | 1.2       | 1          | 1     | 1      |      | 1.4278 | 14.278 |

Duke’s biggest strengths are in its Traditions as a program and for having one of the premier arenas in NCAA College Basketball. Because of that, Duke’s Traditions, Facilities, and Atmosphere attributes are the most impactful attributes as part of the formula.

The average of all of the modifiers becomes 1.1778. Because Testaverde is considered a recruit that’s close to home, a 25% bonus is applied, making the modifier 1.4278

### Example 2

Lindenwood is a fairly new program and is attempting to make waves in recruiting. They are attempting to recruit Seamus O’Conner, a Power Forward based in Minnesota. Here is how the calculation goes:

|                 | Program | Prof. Dev. | Traditions | Facilities | Atmosphere | Academics | Conf. | Coach | Season | CTH? | Avg    | Total |
| :-------------- | ------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- | --------- | ----- | ----- | ------ | ---- | ------ | ----- |
| Lindenwood      | 5       | 5          | 4          | 6          | 2          | 5         | 5     | 5     | 5      | 0    |        |       |
| Seamus O'Conner | 5       | 5          | 2          | 9          | 9          | 5         | 9     | 9     | 5      |      |        |       |
|                 | 1       | 1          | 0.8        | 1.2        | 0.4        | 1         | 1     | 1     | 1      |      |        |       |
|                 | 1       | 1          | 1.2        | 0.7        | 0.3        | 1         | 0.6   | 0.6   | 1      |      | 0.8222 | 8.222 |

Because Lindenwood’s basketball team is just starting, they have fairly new facilities but don’t have the same traditions that many atlantic schools have. Because Seamus deeply cares about playing at a school that offers a fantastic gameday experience – rowdy fans, large arena, his name on the jumbotron; in addition, a program being in a historic conference lead by a coach who knows how to win; the points that Lindenwood spends on Seamus are less impactful. The modifier in this case averages to about 0.8222.

### Player Acquisition - Transfer Portal

The Transfer Portal designed for SimCBB is exactly that of which we have in SimCFB.

Players will announce their intention after progressions run, with coaches given one week to commit a promise to players with the intent of having them stay on their team. Any players that do **not** commit enter the portal.

There will be 10 weeks of the transfer portal, with coaches able to create one promise for each player on their board, and being able to commit up to 10 points per player, with a max of 50 spread across all players.

Users will be able to view the grade attributes of players during the transfer portal.

The decision system will be the same one as which we use for SimCBB recruiting. All teams within 66% of the leading team’s points will be in consideration.

Please promise players at your own discretion. The following types of promises are allowed below:

- Wins for the season
- No redshirt
- Number of minutes played per game
- Winning the conference
- Making it to the post-season tournament
- Making it to the Sweet 16, Elite 8, or Final Four.
- Winning the national championship

Promises are high risk by design. While a player can commit to only one promise at a time, users can make as many promises as they want to any number of players. There's no limit. With that in mind, the coaches are responsible to ensure that the promises are fulfilled within the next season.

During the transfer intention phase, promises are used to retain the player. During the transfer portal phase, promises can be made to add a multiplier to ensure the players you're targeting sign with you. The higher the promise, the higher the multiplier.

### Promise Weights

Promises during the transfer portal can be made to players as a means of making your points submitted on the player more impactful. The larger the weight of the promise, the higher the multiplier and the higher your points will go.  
It should be noted, however, that

### Portal Reputation

Portal Reputation is the final multiplier toward points submissions in this stage. Portal Reputation is a long-term modifier that is designed to reward/deter coaches based on the promises committed onto players through player retention and the transfer portal.

If a coach has a high portal reputation, players will be more likely to consider the points submission of the coach and the promise.

If a coach has a low portal reputation, points submissions on players will be less effective.

The starting portal reputation for a coach is set to 100\. The range for portal reputation values is between 1-120. Meaning that a coach that successfully promises can find benefits; and a coach that has promises fail will struggle.

Portal Reputation will adjust at the end of the next season during the next season’s Transfer Portal Intention Sync. Any promise that succeeds or fails will adjust the reputation of the coach in the following manner:

**Success**:

- Extremely Low: 1 point (if a coach’s reputation is above 100, 0 points)
- Very Low Priority: 3 points (if a coach’s reputation is above 100, 0 points)
- Low Priority: 5 points (if a coach’s reputation is at 100 or above, 1 points)
- Medium Priority: 10 points (If a coach’s reputation is at 100 or above, 3 points)
- High Priority: 15 points (If a coach’s reputation is at 100 or above, 5 points)
- Very High: 20 points (If a coach’s reputation is at 100 or above, 7 points)
- Extremely High: 25 points (If a coach’s reputation is at 100 or above, 10 points)
- National Championship: 30 points (If a coach’s reputation is at 100 or above, 15 points)

**Failure**:

- Extremely Low: \-10 points
- Very Low Priority: \-7 points
- Low Priority: \-5 points
- Medium Priority: \- 10 points
- High Priority: \-20 points
- Very High: \- 25 points
- Extremely High: \- 35 points
- National Championship: \- 45 points

**The case with Extremely Low**: The only category where Extremely Low is available is if the team wins only once during the entire season. If in the event the user does not win one game during the entire regular season, including losing the Toilet Bowl; at this point, the player you made that ridiculous promise to _should_ be disappointed.

### Player Development - Redshirting & Progression

If you’re joining in the off-season, you will have the option to redshirt up to 3-4 players. Redshirted players cannot be assigned minutes for the upcoming season, but will not use up a year of eligibility and will still have a small chance to improve. Any player who hasn’t already been redshirted once (i.e. anyone who does _not_ have parentheses around their year) is eligible for this designation.

At the end of the season, all players progress according to the algorithm covered in [Dev Diary 89](https://www.simfba.com/topic/4271-89-simbba-player-progressions-archetypes-position-update-and-specializations/). Players improve based on the number of minutes they’ve played, their Progression score (reflected in their Potential grade, with some “fuzziness”) and a small random factor. Seniors graduate and, if their Overall is high enough, become available to be drafted into the pro sim.

In addition to the above dev diary, the following should be noted:

- Potential represents the ceiling of growth that a player can reach within a progression. An A rating means that a player will have a great chance at growing. An F rating means that a player’s chance to grow is very low.
- Updated since Dev Diary 89 for college basketball only; if a player does not meet their minutes requirement, their growth will be stunted instead of regressed.

### Scheduling & Game Day

Every year you will have the option to schedule a number of Out of Conference (OOC) games. The exact number will depend on your conference affiliation. You can coordinate with other users to schedule games against their teams, or work with the commissioners to schedule AI-controlled teams from their conference.

Games are run on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays. Results will go up on the interface at 4pm EST on those days and will update the standings as reflected from the results.

For the duration of the season, the SimCBB league lasts for \~20 weeks, with 14 weeks dedicated to the regular season followed by 2 weeks of conference tournaments and 4 weeks of the March Madness tournament. Each SimCBB team plays at least 28 games by the end of the season.

The SimNBA league lasts for \~29 weeks with 21 weeks dedicated to the regular season, followed by 8 weeks of playoffs. The regular season contains about 82 games, like the IRL NBA counterpart.

This concludes the college sim portion. Everything beyond is exclusive to pro basketball.

**Interlude: Media**

As mentioned above, making consistent media is a great way to gain an extra affinity for your program. But it’s also just a way to engage with the sim and provide fun content for other users. SimBBA doesn’t have any pay-to-win components, so there’s no mechanical advantage to being active on Discord or to creating a certain type of media. But some users really enjoy that aspect of the sim, and we encourage people to stay active in as many ways as they can throughout the seasons.

# SimNBA Exclusive Rules

## NBA 1: Contract Rules & Valuation

Every player on an NBA roster has a contract that specifies how long they will play for their current team and how much they will be paid to do so. There are two components to any contract: Salary and Options. **Salary** is how much money you’re giving to a player. It should be noted that **every** contract is considered to be **guaranteed** money. **Options** on the other hand, give teams flexibility in how they want to keep a player. These terms will always be capitalized to remind you of their specific meaning.

To compare contracts of different lengths and Bonus/Salary amounts, the following formula is used:

Each $1M of Salary is worth 1.0 in the first year, and 0.1 less each year thereafter (0.9, 0.8, etc)  
Each Year of Option is worth 0.8 in the first year, and 50% less each year thereafter (0.4, 0.2, etc)

The final number is referred to as the contract’s **Value**. Value is the single defining factor by which all contracts are compared. There can be other things that affect Value, like Free Agency Bias, but by far the biggest driver of Value is money, especially guaranteed money.

All offered contracts must conform to the following rules:

- Duration of at least 1 year, but no more than 5 years
- Minimum total pay of $0.5M every year
- Salary cannot decrease (but can remain flat)
- Total pay cannot increase by more than 50% from one year to the next (or $3M, whichever is higher)
- The highest year's pay cannot be more than double the lowest year's pay (or $6M more, whichever is higher)

The percentages in rules 4 & 5 exist to minimize back-loading of large contracts \- you **cannot** sign a player to a contract of 5/10/25 million over 3 years. The dollar amounts exist to ensure small contacts are still feasible \- you **can** sign a player to a contract of 2/4/6 million over 3 years.

### Cutting Players

Cutting a player immediately places the player on the Waiver Wire. If the player hasn’t been brought up by another team in about a week’s time, they will immediately enter Free Agency. Once they enter free agency, the team that previously held the contract for the player will pay the rest of the contract as dead money for the contract’s former duration.

## NBA 2: Player Acquisition

Players can be added to your team in one of 3 ways: free agency, the draft, or via trade with another team.

### 2a. Free agency

During the offseason, players whose existing contracts have expired enter into free agency and can be acquired by any team. Before free agency opens, players are assigned a target Value they hope to achieve, based on their Overall score and the pay of other similarly talented players at their position. Once the free agency period begins, teams use the interface to submit contract offers that meet or exceed that target- see [Dev Diary 99](https://www.simfba.com/topic/5437-99-all-simcbb-and-simnba-changes-announced-in-the-livestream/) and [Dev Diary 85](https://www.simfba.com/topic/4225-85-interface-free-agency-and-trades/).

All players begin in the “Open” stage, where any team can bid on them. Teams can make as many offers as they want to as many players as they want. Everyday, some time between 10 AM and 12 PM\*, the interface syncs and all bids are processed. If a player hasn’t received any newer or updated bids within a span of three days, the player will go with the offer that provides the most contract value to the player.

_\*The uncertainty of the sync time is to prevent “sniping”, where teams try to win free agents via last-second bids. Alternatives / refinements to this process will be discussed at the next Owners meeting._

You can also attempt to sign players to your Active roster off another team’s Practice Squad (in the Free Agency menu, click “Practice Squad” to see a list of available players). Once an offer is made, the player’s current team will get a notification that they can match it. If they do, the player is promoted to the Active squad of the current team. If they decline, or if 24 hours passes, you sign the player. You must pay the player at least as much as their current team is paying them. You **cannot** sign players from another Practice Squad directly onto your Practice Squad.

### 2b. Draft

The Draft is an opportunity for teams to acquire exclusive rights to the best college players for a predetermined contract amount. The Draft includes 2 rounds over 1 real-time day, with teams having 1 pick in each round (before trades) based on their performance in the previous year. The draft pool is filled with players from SimCBB, so there is continuity between the two sims.

The draft order is determined identically to the real NBA: a lottery will be ran after the SimNBA finals to determine the order from 1-16, followed by reverse order of standings, in order of first round losers (19-24), second round losers (25-28), conference championship losers (29-30), and finally the SimNBA Finals runner-up (31) and champion (32). The only tiebreaker is strength of schedule, with weaker schedules going first.

The draft is handled on the interface. Once the draftable players are loaded in, teams have a pool of scouting points they can use to learn the true values of key attributes. They can also learn a player’s Potential grade, **which is newly re-rolled and different from their college score.** This simulates the unpredictability of the draft and increases the value of good scouting. For full details on the draft page, see [Dev Diary 100](https://www.simfba.com/topic/5441-100-the-simnba-draft-page/) and [Dev Diary 113](https://www.simfba.com/topic/6144-113-simfba-the-draft-page/).

All drafted rookies are automatically signed to a 4-year contract with salary and options based on the below Rookie Pay Scale. It is updated each year based on changes to the Salary Cap, but generally uses several tiers for 1st round picks based on draft position and then a single tier for each subsequent round. For first-round picks only, teams have the option of picking up a third year and fourth year option and automatically extending the contract for one additional year. Teams decide on this option at the end of the drafted player’s 2nd season.

### 2c. Trades

Owners can make trades at any time from the start of the league year (off-season), through free agency, the draft, and game 42 of the NBA season. After the trade deadline is reached, no trades can take place until after the SimNBA Finals, when a new league year starts.

Teams can trade any player on their roster, as well as current & future draft picks. Before the draft, they can trade picks in the upcoming draft and one year out; once the draft begins, they can trade picks from the current draft and two years out.

Traded picks are tracked on the interface, but a graphical representation is also kept up to date [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1B1i2qJx34mclhppcUdkyZYWonNVFSZoxDgXNAV9M5lY/edit?usp=sharing).

When a team trades a player with Bonus money on their contract, any and all Bonus remaining automatically becomes Dead Cap on the old team’s cap sheet, and thus is still counted as being paid by the old team. All Salary switches to the new team, although teams are free to also negotiate Salary payments as part of the trade (for the current year only, and only if there is more than 1 year remaining on the contract). If a player with a 100% Bonus contract is traded, the new team will still need to pay the player $0.5M in Salary; the rules have been changed so that all contracts must have at least $0.5M in Salary each year, but there are still old contracts in existence that are entirely Bonus.

## NBA 3: Salary Cap & Roster Management

The salary cap for 2026 is $165M, and will increase to $170M in 2027\. Future year caps are published two league years in advance. A team’s largest contracts, plus any acquired dead cap or penalties, must always remain below the Salary Cap allotted for that year. Dead cap is accrued by cutting or trading players with unpaid Bonus money; penalties are accrued by breaking league rules, such as putting players on your depth chart who are not on the active roster.

To reduce expenses and stay under the salary cap, teams can cut players or move them to the G-League. To cut a player from your team, just click the scissors icon next to their name on the Roster page, and confirm. All Bonus money will become Dead Cap on the team’s cap sheet, similar to the trade scenario, but Salary will be removed. Always check a player’s current contract to ensure that you are aware of any possible Dead Cap hits.

To demote a player from the Active Roster to the G League, click on the silhouette (far right button) on the Roster page, and confirm. Practice Squad players do not count against your cap, but must pass through waivers (see below) and could be signed away by other teams as mentioned in section 2a above. Players must have 3 or fewer years of Experience to be placed on the Practice Squad.

Cut players with 4 or more years of experience immediately become free agents and are eligible to receive offers to sign with other teams. Cut players with 3 or fewer years of experience are placed on waivers for 48 hours, and teams can put in a waiver claim to sign them at their current contract. If the player receives no offers in 48 hours, they clear waivers and become a free agent.

During the offseason and through the first three weeks of the regular season, the waiver priority order is the same as the most recent year’s draft order. After the third week of the regular season, the waiver priority order reverts to reflect the current NBA standings in reverse order, so that the team with the worst record gets first priority on all waiver claims. The order changes weekly based on record but does NOT change based on claims: the team with first priority remains ‘first in line’ for ALL players that week, no matter how many claims they make.

During the regular season, a team is allowed to have up to 15 players on their active roster and another 16 players on their G-League. During the offseason & preseason, a team may keep up to 30 players on their roster. Just… please don’t hoard players.

## NBA 4: Extensions and tags

Late in the regular season, a team has the opportunity to **extend** players who are currently on the last year of their contract. Extensions enable teams to keep their best players from entering free agency, but at an increased cost befitting the player’s experience and talent. Value demands for all players are updated (just like they are in free agency) but only the player’s current team can make an offer. Offers that meet the requested Value are automatically accepted, but a team can offer as low as 70% of this Value and still have a chance of the player signing.

If a team cannot reach a long-term contract agreement but does not want a player to hit free agency, they can apply a tag to that player. There are two tags: franchise and transition. _This feature is currently in development and will be discussed at the next Owner’s meeting._

## NBA 5: Progression / Regression & Retirement

As with college, the progression algorithm is being rewritten to accommodate for the upgraded attribute system for SimBBA.

## International Super League

The ISL is a secondary professional league consisting of the top international teams outside of the United States and Canada. There are approx. 160 international teams within this league spanning across all continents except Antarctica for very specific reasons. Maybe one day, but not today.

The ISL is designed to emulate not just the Euroleague, but also how global the sport is in general. Many players in the NBA originate from outside the United States, did not play in college, and we wanted to simulate that pathway in a way that we thought made sense. Many stars that we know today played professionally in the Euroleague and in national leagues. Teams within the ISL are directly from those leagues, and are placed in “leagues” or conferences that are regionally relevant to one another.

Rosters within the ISL are mainly made up of players originating outside of the United States, and may also consist of former veteran SimNBA players. Additionally, players generated within the SimNBA may also be younger than the average generated high school recruit in SimCBB. When ISL-generated players that are younger that reach the age of 18/19, they may choose to declare for the SimNBA and immediately become eligible to draft.

ISL Players that have not declared for the SimNBA that are younger than the age of 22 cannot be picked up in SimNBA Free Agency.

At the moment, ISL teams cannot be coached or represented by the user. Users can see game results for these teams, however. We are hoping one day to build out the feature that would allow ISL teams to build talent similar to how soccer/futbol builds its talent: youth leagues. But for now, we don’t have something like that.
